title: Ragi to Kuttu: 5 Healthy Flours for Janmashtami Fasting
excerpt: Nutritionist Dr. Shikha Sharma recommends these traditional Indian flours to make vrat meals nourishing, varied, and lighter than the usual fried fare.
body:
• Five traditional Indian flours — ragi, kuttu (buckwheat), rajgira (amaranth), singhara (water chestnut), and sama rice (barnyard millet) — offer nutritious, gluten-free alternatives to regular wheat during Janmashtami and other Hindu fasts.
  • Kuttu flour is the most widely accepted vrat flour, providing plant-based protein, fiber, and minerals while remaining naturally gluten-free despite its misleading English name.
  • Nutritionist Dr. Shikha Sharma recommends choosing pan-cooked, steamed, or baked preparations over deep-fried versions to keep fasting meals lighter and more healthful.
  • Fasting rules vary across households and regional traditions — devotees should choose flours permitted under their own vrat practices.

Janmashtami fasting is as central to the festival as the midnight celebrations themselves. Millions of devotees across India and the diaspora observe a day-long fast in honor of Lord Krishna's birth, abstaining from regular grains, pulses, and many everyday ingredients. But fasting does not have to mean surviving on fried potatoes and sugar-heavy sweets.

Nutritionist Dr. Shikha Sharma has highlighted several traditional flours that can transform vrat meals from heavy, monotonous affairs into nutritious, varied spreads. These flours have been used in Indian fasting traditions for generations, and each brings its own nutritional profile and culinary versatility to the table.

Five Flours for a Healthier Fast

1. Ragi Flour (Finger Millet)

Ragi is rich in calcium, fiber, and protein, making it one of the most nutritionally complete millet flours available. It supports immune function and has a low glycemic index, which helps prevent the blood sugar spikes that can follow a long fast. Ragi flour can be used to make dosas, idlis, or simple rotis.

One caveat: ragi is not universally accepted as a fasting ingredient across all Hindu traditions. Some households include it in their vrat diet while others consider it a regular grain. Check your family's customs before using it during Janmashtami.

"Millions of devotees across India and the diaspora observe a day-long fast in honor of Lord Krishna's birth, abstaining from regular grains, pulses, and many everyday ingredients."

2. Kuttu Flour (Buckwheat)

Despite its name, buckwheat has no relation to wheat and is naturally gluten-free. Kuttu flour is the most popular and widely accepted vrat flour in North India, used to make puris, parathas, cheelas, and pancakes. It is rich in fiber, high in plant-based protein, and relatively low in calories, while providing meaningful amounts of calcium and magnesium for bone strength.

Dr. Sharma recommends opting for kuttu ka paratha or dosa rather than deep-fried kuttu ke pakore to keep the meal lighter. Pairing kuttu preparations with plain yogurt or permitted vegetables makes for a more balanced plate.

3. Rajgira Flour (Amaranth)

Rajgira, or amaranth flour, is another staple of the Indian fasting kitchen. It is high in protein and fiber, gluten-free, and carries an earthy, slightly nutty flavor that works in both sweet and savory preparations. Use it for vrat rotis, pancakes, or even porridge. Rajgira laddoos made with jaggery and ghee are a popular Janmashtami treat.

For a healthier version, reduce the ghee and substitute powdered jaggery for refined sugar. The flour's natural nuttiness means it needs less added sweetener than wheat-based alternatives.

4. Singhara Flour (Water Chestnut)

Singhara flour, ground from dried water chestnuts, is widely used during fasting periods across India. It is naturally gluten-free and primarily contributes carbohydrates, making it a quick energy source during long fasting days. The flour is also known for helping with water retention and providing potassium and essential micronutrients.

Singhara flour works well for rotis, cheelas, and halwa. Because it has a dense, starchy texture, it pairs best with yogurt, nuts, or seeds that add protein and fat to round out the meal. Keep an eye on portion sizes and cooking methods — singhara puris cooked in excess oil can cancel out the flour's inherent lightness.

5. Sama Rice Flour (Barnyard Millet)

Sama rice, also known as samak ke chawal, is one of the most common fasting grains in Indian households. Ground into flour, it can be used for pancakes, cheelas, or as a porridge base. The millet provides sustained carbohydrate energy and pairs well with curd-based sides.

Sama rice khichdi — made with cumin, green chilies, and peanuts in ghee — remains one of the most satisfying one-pot vrat meals. For variety, try sama rice pulao with permitted vegetables and sendha namak.

Making Fasting Meals More Nutritious

The flour is only one component. Dr. Sharma and other nutritionists emphasize that cooking method matters as much as ingredient choice. Pan-cooking, steaming, and baking are preferable to deep-frying. Combining fasting flours with permitted protein sources — curd, milk, paneer, nuts, and seeds — creates more balanced meals that sustain energy through a long fast.

Hydration is equally important, especially for those not observing nirjala (waterless) fasts. Fresh coconut water, buttermilk, and plain water should be consumed regularly throughout the day.

People with diabetes, kidney conditions, or pregnancy-related nutritional needs should consult a doctor before undertaking extended fasts, regardless of the food choices available.

nri_angle: Diaspora families observing Janmashtami can find kuttu, rajgira, and singhara flours at Indian grocery stores and use these traditional alternatives for healthier fasting meals.
